question: Can scalar activation functions be compared through a finite, affine-aware collection of integral statistics that jointly predicts signal propagation, dynamical stability, bias drift, and induced-kernel regularity?

key_findings.claim: The proposed signature combines five Gaussian statistics with two tail slopes and two regularity quantities, and is well posed for activations of at most polynomial growth with locally integrable derivative.
key_findings.evidence: The paper defines S_sigma(phi)=(m1,g1,g2,m2,eta,alpha+,alpha-,TV(phi'),C(phi)), proves finiteness of the Gaussian coordinates, gives exact affine scaling-and-bias transformation laws, and obtains subsequential closure under uniformly bounded slope variation and tail compensation.

key_findings.claim: A small subset of the signature controls mean-field forward variance and backward perturbation contraction under the paper's Gaussian-input assumptions.
key_findings.evidence: The forward recursion is q_(l+1)=sigma_W^2 m2(sqrt(q_l))+sigma_b^2, while local forward stability depends on the derivative of that map and backward mean-square contraction is certified by sigma_W g2(sqrt(q*))<1. The paper explicitly distinguishes these sufficient stability conditions from a complete account of finite-network training.

key_findings.claim: Derivative moments yield a dimension-free mixed-Hessian bound for the random-feature kernel, and bounded slope variation supplies a coarser uniform bound.
key_findings.evidence: Differentiating K(x,y)=E[phi(w^T x)phi(w^T y)] and applying Cauchy-Schwarz plus Wick's formula gives an operator-norm bound proportional to g4(||x||)g4(||y||); a uniform derivative bound, itself related to TV(phi'), removes the input dimension from the constant.

key_findings.claim: The numerical section validates computation of the five Gaussian coordinates, but does not empirically validate the proposed activation-selection thresholds on trained networks.
key_findings.evidence: For seven activations and sigma in {0.5,1,2}, 160-node Gauss-Hermite estimates agree to at least six significant digits across node counts; the ReLU Monte Carlo cross-check has roughly 1e-4 error. The experiments calculate signature values only, whereas the stated guidance such as g2 approximately below 0.8 and TV(phi') approximately below 5 is not tested against downstream architecture or dataset outcomes.

method.core_idea: Represent an activation by integral quantities selected to cover Gaussian forward/backward propagation, directional tail behavior, and variation of its slope, then express several stability results directly through those coordinates.
method.mechanism: The analysis uses Gaussian integration by parts, affine change-of-variable identities, Helly selection for bounded-variation derivatives, contraction/Lyapunov arguments for scalar recursions, mean-field variance recurrences, and Gaussian moment inequalities for kernel Hessians. Eight common activations are classified analytically and seven receive numerical Gaussian-coordinate estimates.
assumptions: Scalar activations have at most polynomial growth, are almost everywhere differentiable, and have locally integrable derivatives.
Wide-layer preactivations are adequately approximated by centered Gaussian variables at the relevant variance scale.
The random-feature kernel uses isotropic standard-Gaussian weights.
Sufficient contraction and curvature bounds are useful design proxies even though they need not predict end-to-end optimization or generalization.

techniques.role: Unifies Gaussian moments, tail slopes, and derivative regularity in one finite comparison object.
Tracks how every signature coordinate changes under input scaling, bias shifts, output scaling, and offsets.
Connects m2 and g2 to forward fixed-point stability and backward perturbation contraction.
Uses Helly-type convergence to establish closure of activation families under controlled slope variation.
Computes Gaussian expectation coordinates at several input scales and checks them against analytic and Monte Carlo values.

evaluations.setting: Seven activations at Gaussian scales 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0
evaluations.metric: m1, g1, g2, m2, and eta
evaluations.result: The paper reports all five coordinates and qualitative separation between saturating and linear-growth families.
evaluations.baseline: Closed-form ReLU values and analytic activation classifications

evaluations.metric: Relative change across 80, 120, and 160 Gauss-Hermite nodes
evaluations.result: Reported changes between 120 and 160 nodes are below 1e-6 for all tabled values.
evaluations.baseline: 300,000-sample ReLU Monte Carlo check with errors around 1e-4

limitations: The theory is restricted to scalar activations and mostly Gaussian, isotropic, fully connected mean-field settings.
Non-Gaussian, heavy-tailed, anisotropic, attention, residual, and normalization dynamics can require different or additional coordinates.
The link from finite TV(phi') to finite-width generalization is left open.
The numerical study verifies quadrature and taxonomy values rather than causal improvement in network training.
Several design cutoffs in the conclusion are heuristics derived from sufficient bounds, not empirically calibrated universal thresholds.
failure_modes: Two activations can share the nine coordinates at selected scales yet behave differently under a non-Gaussian or multimodal preactivation distribution.
A contraction certificate may be too conservative and reject useful near-critical or deliberately chaotic regimes.
Bias, normalization, and residual paths can invalidate the scalar mean-field recursion used for selection.
Smoothness of the induced infinite-width kernel need not translate to better feature learning in a finite trained network.
reusable_insights: Evaluate an activation as a scale-dependent curve of statistics rather than by a single pointwise property such as smoothness.
Separate forward variance, backward gain, signed bias drift, and kernel curvature when diagnosing activation behavior.
Make activation comparisons invariant-aware by recording how the chosen statistics transform under shifts and rescalings.
Treat analytic certificates as filters to be paired with downstream empirical validation, not as final rankings.
open_questions: Which additional coordinates are necessary and sufficient for residual networks, normalization layers, and attention blocks?
Do empirical preactivation distributions produce more predictive signatures than Gaussian surrogates?
Can two activations with matched proposed signatures be constructed to falsify the signature's practical sufficiency?
How should signature targets be optimized jointly across depth-dependent input scales?
Are the proposed TV and gain heuristics correlated with optimization and generalization across modern architectures?

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Information Propagation
competitive_landscape.difference: Schoenholz et al. derive ordered, chaotic, and critical signal-propagation regimes for random networks; the reviewed paper packages related Gaussian moments together with tail and bounded-variation quantities into an activation-level taxonomy.

competitive_landscape.title: Resurrecting the Sigmoid in Deep Learning through Dynamical Isometry: Theory and Practice
competitive_landscape.difference: Pennington et al. analyze Jacobian spectra and dynamical isometry for specific architectures and initializations; the reviewed work offers coarser moment-based contraction and kernel bounds that compare activation families but do not characterize full singular-value spectra.

competitive_landscape.title: Searching for Activation Functions
competitive_landscape.difference: Ramachandran et al. discover Swish through task-driven search, while the reviewed paper proposes selecting or designing activations by constrained integral coordinates; it does not yet show that the analytic selection procedure beats empirical search.

competitive_landscape.title: Gaussian Process Behaviour in Wide Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Matthews et al. establish wide-network Gaussian-process limits, supplying the distributional setting on which several reviewed-paper recursions depend; the reviewed paper focuses on activation statistics and explicit regularity bounds rather than proving a network limit.

novelty_assessment: The useful novelty is the attempt to make activation comparison affine-aware and multi-criterion by joining Gaussian propagation statistics with tail compensation and bounded variation, plus expressing several sufficient results in that vocabulary. The individual mean-field, dynamical-isometry, kernel, and activation-search ingredients have substantial prior art, and the downstream predictive value of the nine-coordinate package is not established by the numerical quadrature study.
reviewer_notes: Read against the extracted 25-page manuscript, including theorem statements, Tables 1-4, related work, and limitations. Competitor identities and primary arXiv records were checked on 2026-08-23. Mathematical claims here are scoped as sufficient results under the paper's assumptions; the unvalidated practical thresholds are explicitly separated from proved statements.
